name: Jean Lafitte National Historical Park and Preserve
author: author-C-2026-10-08
summary:
The Mississippi River built this country. At the end of its journey it drops sediment scoured from 40 percent of the continental United States, and the ground beneath the New Orleans region is less than 4,000 years old — marsh, slow bayous, cypress swamp and forested natural levees in a restless interplay of land and water. American Indians settled the delta as it formed, some 2,500 years ago; from the 1720s European settlers and enslaved Africans took their place among them, and the park’s brochure traces how French, Chitimacha and Houma, West African, Spanish-speaking Isleño, Caribbean and Acadian peoples together made the culture now called Creole and Cajun. [1]

On January 8, 1815, on the Chalmet plantation below New Orleans, Andrew Jackson’s mixed force of regulars, militia, volunteers and Jean Lafitte’s Baratarian privateers stopped a British assault in less than two hours; more than 2,000 British soldiers were killed, wounded or captured and American casualties numbered fewer than 20. Chalmette National Historical Park, created in 1939 to preserve part of that field, was the first national park unit in Louisiana. Congress expanded it into Jean Lafitte National Historical Park and Preserve on November 10, 1978, and in 1988 added three Acadian cultural centers, for six sites in all. The land itself is now going: blocked sedimentation, subsidence and rising seas cost the delta, by the brochure’s count, a football field’s worth of land every 45 minutes. [1] [2]

climate.html: The delta was always in motion: over 3,500 years the Mississippi built five major deltas, the newest only 500 years old, while subsidence and erosion balanced the new land it laid down. Levees and channelization have broken that balance. The park’s 2015 foundation document says parts of this landscape have the highest rate of relative sea-level rise and land loss in North America — a historical average of 0.36 inches a year at Grand Isle from 1947 to 2012, with projections for 2100 of 3.3 to 7.6 feet. In Barataria Preserve, scientists have already documented species lost from the natural levee ridges, more flooding and land loss, and the document names the climate-driven rise of ocean influence over the delta and its people the park’s major cross-cutting concern. [1] [2]

black.html: Around 1867, Jean Pierre Fazende, a free man of color before emancipation, began selling lots on part of the old Chalmet plantation to freedmen. Fazendeville grew into a close-knit Black working-class village of about 40 houses, a church, stores, a school and benevolent societies, sitting between the battlefield monument and the national cemetery, which for generations drew its laborers from the village. Blythe’s 2012 administrative history records that NPS managers believed from the start that the community would have to be obliterated to restore the historic scene. Congress authorized purchase of every property in 1962, and by 1964 the village was gone — taken, former residents told an anthropologist, while Black residents of St. Bernard Parish were still fighting for the vote. The same history notes that park managers long overlooked the free men of color who fought for Jackson. The NPS placed a wayside about Fazendeville on the battlefield in 2008. [3] [2]

slavery.html: The Barataria basin south of New Orleans was sugar country before the Civil War. In 1850, Holmes’s 1986 historic resource study counts 1,176 people living there: 504 enslaved, 15 free people of color and 657 white, with 79 percent of the enslaved owned by planters and living on the plantations. In 1856 the Mavis Grove plantation inventoried houses for 156 enslaved people alongside its steam sawmill, seventy mules and $226,914 in total value. Enslaved workers labored six days a week, and every day during the October-to-December harvest and grinding season. Jean Lafitte’s smuggling empire in the basin, which the park’s foundation document notes trafficked in enslaved people, was bold enough to advertise auctions of contraband slaves openly. [4] [2]

indigenous.html: People lived in the Barataria basin as soon as the river formed it, and by the Marksville period (about 100 B.C. to A.D. 300) were building large villages, growing corn and probably beans and squash while relying chiefly on hunting, fishing and gathering. Prehistoric shell middens from that long occupation remain part of the preserve’s landscape. At French contact their descendants were the Washa, Chawasha and Chitimacha (“Sitimachas” on a 1718 French map). France’s Indian allies waged a twelve-year war on the Chitimacha which, Holmes writes, supplied the French colony with many Indian slaves from Chitimacha bands; the 1718 peace forced the Chitimacha to abandon Bayou Lafourche and settle near New Orleans. By 1739 the Washa and Chawasha together numbered only thirty warriors, a collapse the study attributes probably to disease. [4] [2]

latino.html: Spain ruled Louisiana from 1763 to 1800, and its colonial government built the road through the preserve still called El Camino Real de Barataria, the royal road. In 1778 the first settlers from the Canary Islands — the Isleños — arrived, brought by the Spanish governor to strengthen Spain’s hold against British and American aggression. In 1779 a group of about 150 settled at the meeting of Bayou des Familles and Bayou Barataria; the bayou’s name, “of the families,” comes from them. Hurricanes and river crevasses wore the settlement down over some sixteen years, until a crevasse that opened in or before 1796 ruined the last five families’ crops and livestock and the government moved them to Terre aux Boeufs, in today’s St. Bernard Parish. [1] [2] [4]
